sceneHappening: Titus brings good news, and godly sorrow leads to joy
summary: Having these promises, Paul urges them to cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. "Open your hearts to us. We wronged no one, we corrupted no one, we took advantage of no one." He says this not to condemn them, for he has said before that they are in his heart, to die together and to live together. "Great is my boldness of speech toward you. Great is my boasting on your behalf. I am filled with comfort. I overflow with joy in all our affliction." When he came into Macedonia, their flesh had no rest: "we were afflicted on every side. Outside were fightings. Inside were fears." But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted them by the coming of Titus, and by the comfort with which Titus was comforted about them, as he told of their longing, mourning, and zeal for Paul. Paul does not regret his letter, even though he regretted it for a time, for it grieved them only for a while. "Now I rejoice, not that you were made sorry, but that you were made sorry to repentance. For you were made sorry in a godly way... For godly sorrow works repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world works death." See what earnestness this godly sorrow produced in them: what eagerness to clear themselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment. In everything they have proved themselves innocent in the matter. Paul wrote not for the sake of the offender or the one wronged, but so that their earnestness for Paul might be made known to them before God. Titus's spirit was refreshed by them all, and what Paul had boasted about them to Titus proved true. "I rejoice that in everything I am of good courage concerning you."
whySettingMatters: Here the story's turning point appears. Paul had sent a painful letter and waited anxiously; now Titus has arrived and the news is better than he feared. Chapter 7 reads like a long breath out, and it fills in what he felt between 2:12-13 and now: the "fightings" and "fears" in Macedonia (7:5). The distinction between godly and worldly grief is one of the most practical in the letter: godly grief leads away from a sin and toward life, while worldly grief just sinks into regret or self-pity. The list of what the Corinthians showed (7:11) reads like an inventory of a church waking up. Notice also what Paul says the letter was for: not to punish a wrongdoer but to reveal the Corinthians' own loyalty. It is not clear whether the Corinthians' repentance was complete or only that of the majority; Paul's later chapters (10 to 13) suggest that some still opposed him, which is one reason scholars debate how the letter fits together.

people.note: Comforted by Titus's report, and rejoicing that the church repented.
Brings good news from Corinth, refreshed by the Corinthians.
Sorrowed in a godly way and showed earnestness.
The one wronged and the wrongdoer, left unnamed.

questions: Paul says godly grief and worldly grief lead in different directions. How can you tell them apart?
Paul admits he first regretted his letter and then did not. What does that say about honest ministry?
Titus's report brought Paul comfort. Who has been a Titus for you?
Paul says the letter's purpose was to show the Corinthians' own earnestness. What does that suggest about the purpose of correction?

"Perfecting holiness in the fear of God" (7:1).

"His affection is more abundantly toward you" (7:15).
"If in anything I have boasted to him" (7:14).
